issues.legal_issue: A lessor may establish that it retook possession of vacant leased land through a site record and the lessee’s unequivocal admission.
material_facts: The lease was terminated and the lessor prepared a panchnama recording that it had taken possession of the vacant plot.
The lessee wrote to the lessor acknowledging that possession had been taken and asking for a refund or for possession to be returned.
The plot was vacant and had wild bushes growing on it; the lower courts had not made a clear finding that possession remained with the lessee.
issues.conclusion: The lessee had been dispossessed pursuant to termination of the lease, and possession had been taken over by the lessor.
issues.legal_principle: Upon termination of the lease, title to the property vested in the lessor, and possession of vacant property followed title. The site panchnama evidenced the takeover, and the lessee’s unequivocal, unconditional admission was compelling evidence of dispossession; the presence of wild bushes did not make the panchnama inconsequential.

rule.if: lease_dispossession_dispute and lease_terminated and vacant_land and (site_recorded_takeover or lessee_admitted_takeover)

predicates.lease_dispossession_dispute: The proceeding concerned whether a lessor had retaken possession after termination of a lease.
predicates.lease_terminated: The lessor terminated the lease of the land.
predicates.vacant_land: The leased land was vacant rather than occupied by a building or active use.
predicates.site_recorded_takeover: The lessor prepared a site record stating that it had taken possession of the land.
predicates.lessee_admitted_takeover: The lessee unequivocally told the lessor that possession had been taken from the lessee.

issues.definition: When a possession dispute follows termination of a lease of vacant land, a site record or the lessee’s unequivocal admission can establish that the lessor retook possession.

issues.legal_issue: A suit seeking a declaration that a lease termination was invalid must be brought within the limitation period measured from when the right to sue first accrued.
material_facts: The lease termination took effect in 1978, and the lessee could have challenged it then, whether or not she had also been dispossessed.
The lessee acknowledged that possession had been taken in 1978.
The transferee filed the declaratory suit in 1996, seeking a declaration that the lease continued to subsist and challenging the termination.
issues.conclusion: The declaratory suit was barred by limitation because it was filed more than three years after the right to sue first accrued.
issues.legal_principle: Article 58 of the Limitation Act, 1963 requires a suit for a declaration not otherwise covered by the Schedule to be filed within three years from when the right to sue first accrues. Under State of Punjab v. Gurdev Singh, Daya Singh v. Gurdev Singh, Bolo v. Koklan, C. Mohammad Yunus v. Syed Unnissa, and Khatri Hotels v. Union of India, that right accrues when the asserted right is infringed or is met by a clear and unequivocal threat; successive violations do not restart time. The right accrued on termination, and even if accrual were measured from dispossession, the suit was still late.

predicates.declaratory_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking a declaration about the continued validity of a lease.
predicates.right_to_sue_first_accrued_on_terminatio: The lease termination first infringed the claimant’s asserted right to have the lease treated as subsisting.
predicates.claim_filed_beyond_limitation_period: The claimant filed the declaratory suit after the applicable limitation period had run from the first accrual of the right to sue.

issues.definition: A declaratory suit is time-barred when the claimant files it after the applicable limitation period has run from the first infringement of the asserted right.

issues.legal_issue: An affected party cannot treat an operative order as invalid and disregard it without obtaining a court’s determination setting it aside or declaring it invalid.
material_facts: The lessor issued an order terminating the lease and acted on it by taking possession of the land.
The claimants argued that the termination was illegal and could be ignored while they sought protection of possession.
No court had set aside or declared invalid the termination order before the claimants sought relief against it.
issues.conclusion: The claimants could not ignore the termination order as non est; they had to seek judicial relief against it, and their asserted possessory rights did not make the late declaratory suit timely.
issues.legal_principle: An order does not bear a visible label of invalidity and remains effective for its ostensible purpose unless the necessary proceedings establish its invalidity. An aggrieved party must seek relief from a competent court within the prescribed limitation period. The Court relied on Smith v. East Elloe Rural District Council, Krishnadevi Malchand Kamathia v. Bombay Environmental Action Group, Pune Municipal Corporation v. State of Maharashtra, R. Thiruvirkolam v. Presiding Officer, State of Kerala v. M.K. Kunhikannan Nambiar, Tayabbhai M. Bagasarwalla v. Hind Rubber Industries, and State of Punjab v. Gurdev Singh. It also held that declaratory relief under the Specific Relief Act is discretionary and that claimed possession could not cure the limitation defect, particularly because possession had been taken over.

rule.if: challenge_to_operative_order and claimant_affected_by_order and order_not_set_aside and claimant_seeks_to_disregard_order_as_invalid

predicates.challenge_to_operative_order: The proceeding concerned a claim against an order that had been issued and acted upon.
predicates.claimant_affected_by_order: The claimant’s asserted rights were affected by the order.
predicates.order_not_set_aside: No competent court had set aside the order or declared it invalid.
predicates.claimant_seeks_to_disregard_order_as_inv: The claimant sought relief on the basis that the order could be treated as invalid without first obtaining a judicial determination against it.

issues.definition: A claimant affected by an operative order cannot disregard it as invalid when no court has set it aside or declared it invalid.
